content: 1. Long COVID, also referred to as Long COVID Syndrome, long-haul COVID, post-COVID-19 condition, post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), or chronic COVID syndrome (CCS), is a condition characterized by persistent symptoms following an acute COVID-19 infection. 2. Studies conducted early in the COVID-19 pandemic revealed that a significant proportion of patients experienced prolonged post-infection sequelae. 3. This condition has been described using various terminologies, including long COVID, long-haul COVID, and post-COVID-19 syndrome, among others. 4. The lack of universally standardized terminology has complicated the characterization of its epidemiology, risk factors, clinical features, and potential treatment options. 5. Symptoms of long COVID can manifest as a combination of respiratory, cardiovascular, urological, neurological, and/or gastrointestinal issues. 6. The most commonly reported symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath (dyspnea), and cognitive dysfunction, often referred to by patients as brain fog. 7. Symptoms may either emerge after the initial recovery from an acute COVID-19 episode or persist from the initial illness. 8. These symptoms can fluctuate or relapse over time, adding to the complexity of the condition. 9. The term Long COVID was first introduced as a hashtag on Twitter by a patient who was not recovering from COVID-19, and it quickly gained acceptance among both the public and medical professionals. 10. Currently, the condition is recognized under various names, including long COVID, long-haul COVID, post-COVID-19 condition, and chronic COVID syndrome. 11. Since September 2020, the condition has been classified in the ICD-10 system as post-COVID-19 condition. 12. On October 6, 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) released a clinical case definition for post-COVID-19 condition using a robust, protocol-based methodology (Delphi consensus), involving diverse stakeholders, including patients, researchers, and experts. 13. According to the WHO, post-COVID-19 condition occurs in individuals with a history of probable or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, typically three months from the onset of COVID-19, with symptoms lasting at least two months and not attributable to an alternative diagnosis. 14. Common symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath, and cognitive dysfunction, which significantly impact daily functioning. 15. Symptoms may be new-onset following recovery from acute COVID-19 or persist from the initial illness, and they may fluctuate or relapse over time. 16. A separate definition may apply to children, and there is no minimum number of symptoms required for diagnosis, although symptoms involving multiple organ systems have been described. 17. The exact pathophysiology of long COVID remains unclear, but several mechanisms have been proposed, including long-term tissue damage, ongoing inflammation, viral persistence, and autoimmunity. 18. Long-term tissue damage may result in persistent symptoms in various organs. For example, lung fibrosis can cause respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea and cough, while structural and metabolic abnormalities in the brain may lead to neurological symptoms like headache, memory loss, and fatigue. 19. Chronic fatigue in long COVID is a complex syndrome potentially linked to autonomic nervous system dysfunction, inflammation, channelopathies, or inadequate cerebral perfusion. 20. Cardiovascular symptoms, such as chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia, may result from cardiac injury during acute COVID-19 episodes, including myocardial inflammation and impaired contractile function. 21. Damage to intrathoracic chemoand mechanoreceptors, which regulate respiration and heart rate, may also contribute to cardiovascular and respiratory symptoms. 22. Ongoing inflammation in long COVID may stem from viral persistence in the gastrointestinal tract, as studies have shown the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in gastric and intestinal cells after recovery from acute COVID-19. 23. Increased fecal shedding of the virus has been observed in some studies, potentially triggering immune activation and systemic inflammation, which may explain the high prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms in long COVID patients. 24. Lymphopenia and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, IL-6, D-dimer) during acute COVID-19 episodes have been associated with long COVID symptoms, particularly myalgia, fatigue, and joint pain. 25. Autoimmunity has also been suggested as a mechanism, with T-cell and B-cell dysfunction potentially promoting long COVID pathophysiology similar to autoimmune diseases. 26. Exercise intolerance in long COVID has been linked to reduced peak aerobic capacity, impaired systemic oxygen extraction, and abnormal ventilatory efficiency, as demonstrated in studies using invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (iCPET). 27. Epidemiological studies have reported varying prevalence rates of long COVID due to differences in terminology and definitions. A meta-analysis estimated that 80% of patients with SARS-CoV-2 infections developed at least one long-term symptom. 28. Women appear to be more commonly affected by long COVID than men, and risk factors may include older age, female gender, pre-existing comorbidities (e.g., obesity, asthma), and greater severity of the acute COVID-19 episode. 29. Even patients with mild initial COVID-19 episodes who did not require hospitalization may experience persistent symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition. 30. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for long COVID, and its natural history, complications, and prognosis are not yet fully understood. 31. Long COVID symptoms can involve almost every organ system, with common physical symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, cough, chest discomfort, and anosmia. 32. Neurocognitive symptoms, such as memory impairment and cognitive dysfunction (brain fog), as well as psychological symptoms like anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), are also frequently reported. 33. Less common symptoms include sweating, myalgias, diarrhea, hair loss, joint pain, sicca syndrome, rhinitis, dysgeusia, poor appetite, dizziness, vertigo, and insomnia. 34. Physical examination findings in patients with cardiopulmonary symptoms may include coarse crackles (suggestive of fibrosis), dullness on percussion (indicative of pleural effusion or consolidation), egophony (a sign of consolidation), and fine basilar crackles (suggestive of pulmonary edema). 35. Cardiac examination findings may include jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, orthostasis, murmurs, pericardial rub, and third or fourth heart sounds. 36. There are no specific diagnostic laboratory findings associated with long COVID, and symptoms do not correlate with SARS-CoV-2 serology. 37. Diagnostic imaging, such as chest X-rays, echocardiography, or CT scans, may be necessary in selected patients to evaluate pulmonary or cardiac complications.
